title: Before You Say “I Do,” There Is One Conversation That Could Save Your Marriage
paragraphs:
Before You Say “I Do,” There Is One Conversation That Could Save Your Marriage
The Question Most Engaged Couples Avoid—Yet Scripture Shows It May Be the Difference Between Lifelong Covenant and Lifelong Regret
Two people can spend years planning a wedding and only a few hours preparing for a marriage.

They can compare venues, flowers, photographers, invitations, honeymoon destinations, and color palettes... while quietly avoiding the conversations that will eventually determine whether they flourish together—or slowly drift apart.
Many couples assume love will solve everything.
Scripture never says that.
The Bible teaches something deeper.
Love is not sustained by emotion alone.
Love is sustained by truth, sacrifice, forgiveness, repentance, humility, and complete surrender to Jesus Christ.
That is why every engaged couple needs to discuss one question before saying, "I do."
Not where you'll live.
Not how many children you'll have.
Not who manages the finances.
Not even your career goals.
Those conversations matter.
But there is something even more foundational.
The question is this:
Will Christ truly be the Lord of our marriage—or only a guest invited to our wedding?
That question changes everything.
Because marriage was never created merely to make two people happy.
Marriage exists to glorify God.
The first pages of Scripture reveal this beautiful design.
Genesis declares:
"Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh." (Genesis 2:24)
The Hebrew expression for "hold fast" is דָּבַק (dāḇaq).
It means far more than simply staying together.
It carries the idea of clinging, adhering, pursuing with unwavering loyalty, being permanently joined together.
It describes covenant.
Not convenience.
Not temporary affection.
Not conditional commitment.
A covenant.
That is why Jesus later quoted this passage in Matthew 19.
He added these unforgettable words:
"What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate."
Marriage begins with God before it ever begins with us.
If Christ is removed from the center, the covenant begins carrying a weight it was never designed to bear.
Many relationships collapse because each person quietly expects the other to become what only Jesus can be.
The perfect comfort.
The perfect provider.
The perfect healer.
The perfect source of identity.
The perfect forgiver.
The perfect satisfaction.
No human being can carry that burden.
Only Christ can.
The Greek New Testament repeatedly describes Jesus as Κύριος (Kyrios)—"Lord."
Not merely teacher.
Not merely Savior.
Lord.
Master.
Supreme Authority.
Every engaged couple should ask one another:
"Will Jesus truly be our Kyrios?"
Because eventually one spouse will disappoint the other.
One will fail.
One will sin.
One will say something careless.
One will struggle.
One may battle fear.
One may experience seasons of doubt.
One may lose a job.
One may become sick.
One may grow spiritually dry.
If Christ is not Lord, those moments often become breaking points.
If Christ is Lord, they become opportunities for grace.
The Apostle Paul paints perhaps the greatest picture of Christian marriage in Ephesians 5.
He doesn't begin with romance.
He begins with surrender.
"Submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ." (Ephesians 5:21)
The word translated "submit" comes from the Greek ὑποτάσσω (hypotassō).
It was never intended to describe domination.
It means willingly placing oneself under God's designed order out of love and devotion.
The passage never portrays marriage as a competition.
It portrays it as mutual sacrifice under the authority of Christ.
Paul then compares marriage to the relationship between Christ and His Church.
That comparison should humble every husband.
It should comfort every wife.
Jesus never ruled His Bride through selfishness.
He loved sacrificially.
He washed feet.
He forgave sinners.
He carried a cross.
He laid down His own life.
That is biblical leadership.
Not power.
Not control.
Sacrificial love.
Likewise, the Church responds to Christ not because He manipulates, but because His love transforms.
This is why every engaged couple should discuss forgiveness before discussing furniture.
Because eventually forgiveness will be needed.
Not once.
Thousands of times.
The Greek word χάρις (charis) means grace.
Grace is God's undeserved favor.
Grace says:
"I know you failed.
I know you hurt me.
I know you aren't perfect.
But because Christ has shown mercy to me, I will choose forgiveness instead of revenge."
Without grace, marriages keep score.
With grace, marriages keep growing.
Then there is repentance.
The New Testament repeatedly calls believers to μετάνοια (metanoia).
Many think repentance simply means feeling guilty.
It does not.
The Greek word literally describes a change of mind that produces a changed life.
Repentance is transformation.
Healthy marriages are not built by perfect people.
They are built by people who repent quickly.
Who apologize sincerely.
Who seek reconciliation humbly.
Who refuse to let pride become a permanent resident inside the home.
One of the greatest dangers for engaged couples is assuming conflict means incompatibility.
Scripture teaches something different.
Conflict often reveals where Christ still wants to transform us.
James writes:
Imagine if every disagreement began with listening instead of defending.
Imagine if every argument ended with prayer instead of silence.
Imagine if every failure ended with repentance instead of resentment.
Imagine a marriage where both spouses compete—not to win arguments—but to outdo one another in showing Christlike love.
That kind of marriage becomes a testimony.
Not because it never struggles.
Because Jesus keeps rewriting it.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
We all entered God's story through scandal.
Sin.
Failure.
Brokenness.
Rebellion.
Yet the cross declares something astonishing.
Jesus specializes in rewriting stories that seemed beyond redemption.
Peter denied Christ.
David committed adultery and murder.
Rahab was known for prostitution.
The Samaritan woman carried the shame of multiple broken relationships.
Paul persecuted Christians.
None of those stories ended with scandal.
They ended with grace.
That is why our theme remains eternally true:
Perhaps you are engaged while carrying hidden fears.
Perhaps one of you has a painful past.
Perhaps there are family wounds.
Financial uncertainty.
Trust issues.
Regret.
Pornography.
Anxiety.
Addiction.
Shame.
Past abortions.
Broken homes.
None of those should be hidden behind smiling engagement photos.
Bring them into the light.
Not because they define your future.
Because Jesus redeems what is surrendered to Him.
John writes:

The Greek word ὁμολογέω (homologeō) means "to confess," literally "to say the same thing." True confession agrees with God about our sin instead of minimizing or excusing it. Forgiveness is never earned by confession; it is granted because of Christ's finished work on the cross, received by faith. That is why confession is an act of hope, not despair.
The strongest marriages are not those with the least brokenness.
They are those where brokenness continually meets the grace of Christ.
If you are preparing for marriage, don't simply ask whether you love one another.
Ask whether both of you are willing to become more like Jesus.
Ask whether Scripture—not feelings—will become your highest authority.
Ask whether prayer will be your first response instead of your last resort.
Ask whether repentance will be practiced regularly.
Ask whether forgiveness will remain open.
Ask whether Christ will always occupy the center.
Because if Jesus is truly Lord of your marriage, every season—even suffering—can become another chapter of redemption.
Someone reading this right now needed this reminder.
Not because your relationship is perfect.
Not because it is falling apart.
But because God is inviting you to build on the only foundation that cannot be shaken.

Share one word that describes what you want God to build in your future or current marriage—"Faithfulness," "Grace," "Trust," "Purity," "Healing," or simply, "Jesus." Your testimony may become the encouragement another couple desperately needs today.
Sometimes God uses an ordinary share to begin an extraordinary conversation that changes a family's future for generations.
God's Word remains true long after emotions change.
Because the wedding lasts a day.
The covenant shapes eternity.
